Reading sources in only 30 minutes is also too short, and citations are left for the last 30 minutes.

plan.taskTitle: Write a 10-page WWI causes research paper due Friday
plan.analysis: Break the paper into parallel research and writing tracks, prioritizing quick source gathering followed by outline-driven drafting to avoid perfectionist revision cycles.

steps.title: Set research scope and find 5-6 sources
steps.description: Spend 20 focused minutes identifying the main causes of WWI (alliances, imperialism, militarism, nationalism) and locate 3-4 academic sources plus 1-2 reliable websites. Don't read deeply yet—just bookmark and skim introductions. Rough notes are fine.

steps.title: Create a detailed outline with thesis
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes structuring your paper: intro with thesis, 3-4 body sections (each covering one major cause), conclusion. Write 1-2 sentence notes under each section. This is your scaffold—it doesn't need to be perfect, just clear enough to write from.

steps.title: Speed-read sources and take rough notes
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes skimming your sources for evidence supporting each outline section. Write messy bullet points directly into your outline. Prioritize speed over polish—you're collecting ammunition, not crafting prose.

steps.title: Draft introduction and first two body sections
steps.description: Write pages 1-4 in one sitting without editing. Aim for roughly 500 words per section. Your first draft will be rough and that's the goal—just move from outline to prose. Stop when you've covered two causes thoroughly.

steps.title: Draft final two body sections and conclusion
steps.description: Continue drafting pages 5-10 using your outline and notes. Write quickly, reference your sources informally (you'll clean up citations later), and finish the conclusion. Done is better than perfect—aim for complete over polished.

steps.title: Read through once and fix major gaps
steps.description: Read your full draft once without stopping. Mark any sections that feel too short or unclear. Spend 20 minutes adding 1-2 sentences to weak spots and smoothing the worst transitions. Don't rewrite—just patch.

steps.title: Format, cite, and proofread lightly
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes adding proper citations to your sources, formatting headings, and doing a quick spell/grammar check. Accept that it won't be flawless—aim for professional, not pristine. Submit with confidence.

plan.taskTitle: Master Organic Chemistry Chapters 5-9 for Midterm Exam
plan.analysis: Break down comprehensive review into daily bite-sized study sessions focusing on one chapter at a time, then practice problems and active recall to build confidence.

steps.title: Skim Chapter 5 and Create Quick Summary
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes quickly reading through Chapter 5, highlighting key reactions and mechanisms. Write 3-4 bullet points about main concepts. Don't worry about understanding everything perfectly—you're just getting familiar with what's there.

steps.title: Deep Dive Chapter 5 with Practice Problems
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes working through 4-5 practice problems from Chapter 5. It's okay if you get some wrong; that's how you learn. Focus on understanding one problem fully rather than rushing through many.

steps.title: Quick Review Chapters 6-7 and Work One Problem Per Chapter
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes reviewing Chapters 6-7 (15 min each), then do just 1-2 practice problems per chapter. You don't need to be thorough here—just identify the main mechanisms and test your understanding.

steps.title: Tackle Chapter 8 with Focused Study
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes on Chapter 8, which often has tricky synthesis problems. Read the key concepts and work through 2-3 practice problems. Rough understanding is fine; mastery comes with repetition.

steps.title: Review Chapter 9 and Identify Connections
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes reading Chapter 9 and noting how it connects to earlier chapters. Do 2 practice problems. You're building a web of understanding, not memorizing isolated facts.

steps.title: Cumulative Problem Set (Mixed Chapters)
steps.description: Spend 35 minutes working on 6-8 mixed problems from all chapters 5-9. This is where everything clicks together. Don't stress about getting them all right; focus on which concepts you still need to revisit.

steps.title: Quick Concept Check and Confidence Builder
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes doing a final review: make a one-page cheat sheet of the 10 most important reactions/concepts, then redo your 2 favorite (or most challenging) problems from the problem set. You've got this!
steps.when: Monday or Tuesday morning before exam

plan.taskTitle: Complete Calculus Problem Set 4 (12 problems) by tomorrow

steps.title: Open the problem set and pick one easy problem

steps.title: Solve the first 3 problems
steps.description: Work through the 3 easiest problems you identified. Don't worry about showing perfect work—just get the answers and basic steps down. This builds confidence and momentum.

steps.title: Take a break and come back for problems 4-6

steps.title: Finish problems 7-9 before bed
steps.description: Tackle 3 more problems before you sleep. At this point you're very close to done. These should feel easier since you've warmed up.

steps.title: Complete the final 3 problems

steps.title: Customize and submit application #1

steps.title: Vacuum or sweep finale
steps.description: Give the floor a final clean with vacuuming or sweeping. This is the satisfying final touch that transforms the whole room. Aim for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Small details polish

steps.title: Draft slides 1-5 (foundation slides)

steps.title: Draft slides 6-10 (strategy and conclusion)

steps.title: Review content and refine language
steps.description: Read through all slides for clarity, accuracy, and flow. Fix grammar and spelling. Ensure each slide has a clear message. Remove redundancy between slides.

steps.title: Practice presentation and finalize

plan.taskTitle: Read chapters 3-4 of The Great Gatsby and write a 1-page response essay
plan.analysis: Break the reading and writing into focused sprints with varied activities to maintain engagement—alternate between reading, note-taking, and drafting to avoid monotony.

steps.title: Speed-read Chapter 3 with active annotations
steps.description: Set a timer for 20 minutes and read Chapter 3, marking key moments (Gatsby's party, Nick's observations, interesting details). Don't aim for perfection—just capture what stands out. This chapter moves quickly and has vivid party scenes.

steps.title: Speed-read Chapter 4 with active annotations
steps.description: Set a timer for 20 minutes and read Chapter 4 (Gatsby's backstory reveal, the Buchanans' drama). Same approach—mark interesting moments and reactions. The plot moves fast here, so it should feel engaging.

steps.title: Brainstorm and outline response (15 minutes)

steps.title: Write first draft of 1-page response

plan.taskTitle: Complete and file your 2026 tax return by April 15, 2027
plan.analysis: Break down tax filing into manageable chunks starting with gathering documents, then organizing information, followed by actual filing using simple tools or professional help.

steps.title: Gather your tax documents in one place
steps.description: Find and collect all documents you'll need: W-2s, 1099s, receipts for deductions, mortgage interest statements, or any other income documents. Just pile them up in one folder—no organizing yet!

steps.title: Make a quick checklist of what you have
steps.description: Write down what documents you found and what income sources you have (job, freelance, investments, etc.). This is just a rough list—not perfect, just enough to see what you're working with.

steps.title: Decide on your filing method
steps.description: Pick one: use free software like IRS Free File or TaxAct, use a paid service like TurboTax, or find a local tax professional. Just decide—no need to overthink it.

steps.title: Set up your chosen tax software or schedule a professional

plan.taskTitle: Write a personal statement for medical school applications
plan.analysis: Break the statement into manageable drafting phases with explicit permission to prioritize completion over perfection, since perfectionist procrastinators often get stuck revising early drafts.

steps.title: Brainstorm core narrative and why medicine
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes listing 3-5 key life experiences that shaped your interest in medicine. Don't worry about how they connect yet—just dump ideas. Rough notes are fine.

steps.title: Identify your unique angle
steps.description: Review your brainstorm and circle the one experience or theme that feels most authentically YOU and different from typical med school applicants. Write 2-3 sentences about why this angle matters. Imperfect is okay.

steps.title: Write a rough zero-draft
steps.description: Set a timer for 30 minutes and write a very messy first draft—aim for 500+ words without stopping to edit. Ignore grammar, redundancy, and polish. The goal is to get words on paper, not perfection.

steps.title: Read for flow and clarity
steps.description: Read your draft aloud once. Highlight sections that feel weak or unclear. Make basic edits (fix obvious typos, cut redundant phrases). Don't rewrite yet—just surface-level fixes.

steps.title: Cut and strengthen weak sections
steps.description: Focus on 2-3 sections that felt weakest. Replace vague language with specific details and examples. Aim for clarity over eloquence. Done beats perfect.

steps.title: Get peer or mentor feedback
steps.description: Share your draft with one trusted person (teacher, mentor, or friend familiar with med school). Ask for 2-3 specific comments, not a full critique. This saves you from over-revising in isolation.

steps.title: Incorporate feedback and final polish
steps.description: Make 3-4 key changes based on feedback. Do a final read-through for tone and grammar. Aim for 'strong and ready' not 'flawless'—medical schools value authenticity over perfection.

steps.title: Final review and submit
steps.description: One last read-through for any glaring errors. Check word count and formatting requirements. Submit. Resist the urge to tweak further.

grade.notes: Seven steps is over-fragmented for a short email; subject, greeting and closing could each be folded into one step. The plan also never has the student open or re-read the professor's original email, so the reply isn't grounded in it (and "Open a blank email draft" is not a reply). Every step is marked "Right now" with no time anchor, which gives an avoider nothing to hold them to a send-by time.

plan.taskTitle: Draft and send professor email requesting assignment extension
plan.analysis: For an avoider procrastinator, we'll start with the smallest possible action—just opening the email—then build momentum through quick, concrete steps that feel easy to complete.

steps.title: Open a blank email draft
steps.description: No pressure—just open your email client and start a new message to your professor. Don't write anything yet, just get the blank page open. This removes the biggest barrier for avoiders.

steps.title: Add the subject line
steps.description: Type a simple, clear subject like 'Request for Extension on [Assignment Name]' or 'Extension Request—[Assignment]'. Keep it straightforward and professional.

steps.title: Write a casual opening greeting
steps.description: Just start with 'Hi Professor [Name],' or 'Dear Professor [Name],'. This gets you writing without any pressure—it's the easiest part.

steps.title: Draft the main request in simple terms
steps.description: In 2-3 sentences, explain that you need an extension and why (be honest but brief—don't over-explain). Example: 'I'm writing to ask for a few extra days on the [assignment]. I've hit an unexpected [obstacle], but I'm committed to turning in quality work.' A rough first draft is totally fine.

steps.title: Add a closing and signature
steps.description: Wrap up with something like 'Thank you for considering my request' and sign with your name. Simple and done.

steps.title: Quick read-through
steps.description: Skim the email once for typos and tone. You don't need it to be perfect—just make sure it makes sense and sounds respectful. If it's good enough, that's good enough.

steps.title: Send the email
steps.description: Hit send. Don't overthink it. Your professor will appreciate you reaching out proactively, and the sooner you send it, the sooner you might get a response.

grade.notes: The first step bundles browsing the website, reading news and choosing 3 accomplishments, which is a 20-minute task that requires decisions and isn't tiny for an overwhelmed student. plan.taskTitle: Master Deloitte interview preparation with behavioral and case practice
plan.analysis: Break down interview prep into focused daily segments covering behavioral storytelling, case interview frameworks, company research, and mock interview practice to build confidence and competence before next Thursday.

steps.title: Research Deloitte and identify 3 key stories
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes browsing Deloitte's website and recent news. Write down 3 accomplishments from your background that align with their values (teamwork, problem-solving, client impact). Don't make these perfect—rough bullet points are totally fine.

steps.title: Learn the STAR method for behavioral questions
steps.description: Watch a 15-minute YouTube video on the STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Write down the structure on a notecard. This is your foundation—just understand the pattern, not perfection.

steps.title: Practice and record one STAR story
steps.description: Pick one of your 3 stories and tell it out loud using STAR format. Record yourself on your phone (audio only). Listen back once. This feels awkward but gets easier fast. Rough delivery is completely okay.

steps.title: Learn case interview basics
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes learning the 4-step case framework: clarify the question, structure your approach, analyze the data, synthesize your recommendation. Write these steps where you can see them. You don't need to be an expert yet—just know the roadmap.

steps.title: Walk through one sample case interview
steps.description: Find one easy case on CaseCoaches or similar site (aim for 15-20 minutes long). Work through it step-by-step using your framework. Don't worry about the 'perfect' answer—focus on following the structure and thinking out loud.

steps.title: Practice second STAR story and refine first
steps.description: Tell your second story using STAR, record it. Then re-record your first story—you'll notice it flows better. Each repetition reduces anxiety. Aim for clear and natural, not polished.

steps.title: Do a full mock interview (behavioral + one case)
steps.description: Ask a friend or mentor to do a 30-minute mock interview: 2-3 behavioral questions + 1 case question. You don't need to be perfect—this is practice in a safe space to build comfort and identify what needs work.

steps.title: Review, adjust, and final prep
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes reviewing your STAR stories and case framework. Identify one thing that felt shaky and practice it once more. Then take a break. You've done substantial work, and you're ready.

plan.taskTitle: Complete Bio 201 enzyme kinetics lab report

steps.title: Organize experimental data and results

steps.title: Calculate kinetic parameters (Km and Vmax)
steps.description: Perform Lineweaver-Burk plot analysis or Michaelis-Menten calculations using your data; include all mathematical work and intermediate steps.

steps.title: Write methods and results sections
steps.description: Document your experimental procedure, equipment used, and present your data with appropriate scientific language; include figure captions for any graphs.

steps.title: Write introduction and analysis discussion
steps.description: Explain enzyme kinetics background, state your hypothesis, analyze your results in context of enzyme behavior, and discuss sources of error or limitations.

steps.title: Create figures and format references
steps.description: Generate publication-quality graphs (Michaelis-Menten and Lineweaver-Burk plots), create a reference list in proper citation format, and ensure all figures are numbered and labeled.

steps.title: Write conclusion and final proofread
steps.description: Summarize key findings, state conclusions about enzyme kinetics, proofread entire document for grammar and clarity, and verify formatting consistency throughout.

plan.taskTitle: Plan and execute surprise birthday party for 15 people by October 24

steps.title: Lock in core details quickly

steps.title: Scout and book the venue
steps.description: Visit or call your top 2 venue choices, confirm availability for your target date, and lock in the booking. This removes the biggest variable and gives you solid footing. Get confirmation in writing.

steps.title: Design the surprise element and theme
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes brainstorming what makes this party memorable—a fun theme, decorations, or a surprise guest. Pinterest or quick Pinterest scroll counts. Pick one creative element that excites you and write it down; don't overthink it.

steps.title: Create guest list and send invites

steps.title: Plan the food and drinks

plan.taskTitle: Plan and execute apartment move by end of October
plan.analysis: Break the move into manageable phases: planning/inventory, finding new place, notifying landlord, packing room-by-room, coordinating logistics, and final cleanup.

steps.title: List what you own and decide what to keep
steps.description: Walk through your apartment for 20 minutes and jot down major items you have (furniture, appliances, boxes of stuff). Don't overthink it—just list the big things. This will calm your mind by giving you a clear picture of what needs to move.

steps.title: Find your new place or confirm move details
steps.description: If you don't have a new place yet, spend 30 minutes looking at 3-4 options online or make calls. If you already have one, just confirm the move-in date and get the address/access details in writing. One small task, totally doable.

steps.title: Notify landlord and document apartment condition
steps.description: Send a brief email or call your landlord to tell them you're moving out by October 31st. Take 5 quick photos of the apartment's current condition on your phone (for your records). This locks in your timeline and removes that anxiety.

steps.title: Gather boxes and packing supplies
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes collecting boxes from your grocery store, online, or asking neighbors. You don't need fancy supplies—boxes are boxes. This is the easiest "real" move-related task and gives you momentum.

steps.title: Pack one room completely (not the kitchen or bedroom)
steps.description: Pick your bathroom, closet, or living room—somewhere small. Set a timer for 45 minutes and pack just that one room into boxes. Label them as you go. One room done = huge confidence boost.

steps.title: Pack remaining rooms in sections
steps.description: Break this into 3 separate sessions: (1) bedroom closet/drawers, (2) kitchen, (3) everything else. Each session is 45 minutes. Spacing them out makes it feel light instead of overwhelming.

steps.title: Arrange movers or recruit friends; confirm logistics
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes booking movers or texting friends to help. Get addresses, times, and contact info all written down in one place. Having a plan takes away the chaos feeling.

steps.title: Final packing, cleaning, and move-out walkthrough

plan.taskTitle: Build practical Spanish conversational skills for traveling in Mexico
plan.analysis: Create a varied learning plan mixing interactive apps, real-world scenarios, and cultural context to stay engaged while building travel-ready Spanish fluency.

steps.title: Quick-start with travel phrases
steps.description: Spend 20 focused minutes on Duolingo or Babbel learning essential travel phrases (greetings, ordering food, asking for directions). Keep it snappy—don't aim for perfection, just get familiar with sounds and basic patterns.

steps.title: Listen to Spanish travel podcasts
steps.description: Find a fun travel-themed Spanish podcast (try "Coffee Break Spanish" or "Pimsleur Spanish") and listen to 2-3 episodes during a commute or workout. Rough understanding is fine—just tune your ear to the rhythm and common words.

steps.title: Create a personalized cheat sheet
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes writing down 30-40 phrases YOU actually need (hotel check-in, menu items you like, pharmacist visit, emergency phrases). Keep it messy and practical—this is for you, not a textbook.

steps.title: Practice speaking with shadowing
steps.description: Pick 3 short YouTube videos of Spanish speakers in real situations (ordering food, shopping, asking directions). Spend 30 minutes playing clips and repeating after them. Your accent won't be perfect—that's the whole point of practice.

steps.title: Try a conversation exchange app

steps.title: Gamify with interactive scenarios

steps.title: Mock travel role-play practice
steps.description: Grab a friend or family member and do 20 minutes of casual role-play (you order at a restaurant in Spanish, they run it; then swap). Laugh at mistakes—that's how you learn, and it keeps energy high.

steps.title: Quick review sprint and confidence check
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes reviewing your cheat sheet, listening to one podcast episode again, and using a speech-recognition app (Google Translate's voice feature) to test your pronunciation. You don't need to be fluent—just confident enough to try!

plan.taskTitle: Debug and fix linked list node deletion in CS 106 assignment
plan.analysis: Systematically identify the deletion bug through code review and testing, then implement the fix with verification.

steps.title: Review deletion function code
steps.description: Carefully read through your linked list delete function, looking for common issues like improper pointer updates, memory leaks, or incorrect null checks.

steps.title: Create a minimal test case
steps.description: Write a simple test that reproduces the node loss bug—e.g., create a list with 3-5 nodes and delete from different positions (head, middle, tail) to isolate where nodes disappear.

steps.title: Trace through deletion logic by hand
steps.description: Use pen and paper or a debugger to step through one failing test case, drawing the pointer changes before and after each operation to spot the broken logic.

steps.title: Identify and fix the bug
steps.description: Implement the fix (likely missing pointer reassignments, incorrect prev/next updates, or improper head pointer handling) based on your trace.

steps.title: Test all deletion cases
steps.description: Run your test cases again, covering delete at head, middle, tail, single node, and empty list scenarios to confirm the fix works.

steps.title: Run full assignment test suite
steps.description: Execute any provided test harness or your own comprehensive tests to ensure the fix doesn't break other linked list operations (insert, traverse, etc.).

steps.title: Final review and submit
steps.description: Do a final code review for clarity, add comments if needed, and submit before 11:59 PM.

plan.taskTitle: Write a 500-word discussion post on the bystander effect for Psych 101
plan.analysis: Break the writing process into research, outlining, drafting (imperfect is fine), and refining stages to avoid perfectionist paralysis and deliver a solid post by Sunday.

steps.title: Gather bystander effect sources and notes
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes skimming 2-3 reliable sources (textbook, Stanford Encyclopedia, Psychology Today article) on the bystander effect. Jot down key points: definition, Kitty Genovese case, diffusion of responsibility, social inhibition. Don't worry about perfect notes—bullet points are fine.

steps.title: Create a rough outline
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes outlining your post structure: intro with hook, 2-3 main points (definition + examples, key studies, real-world implications), conclusion. This rough outline is your thinking tool—it doesn't need to be polished.

steps.title: Write a messy first draft
steps.description: Set a timer for 30 minutes and write the entire 500-word post without stopping. Aim for 'rough draft is fine'—don't edit, don't perfect word choice, just get ideas down. Aim for roughly 500 words but don't stress if it's 450-550.

steps.title: Read through and note gaps
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes reading your draft once. Identify 1-2 sentences that feel weak or confusing. Don't rewrite yet—just mark them with brackets or highlighting. This helps you see what actually needs fixing versus what feels 'not perfect enough.'

steps.title: Revise weak spots and tighten language
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes rewriting the marked sections and smoothing any awkward transitions. Check that examples are clear and your argument flows logically. This is light editing, not perfecting—aim for 'good enough' not 'flawless.'

steps.title: Final proofread and format check
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes doing a final read for typos, grammar, and formatting. Ensure citations are included if required. Done is better than perfect—submit after this quick pass even if you spot a sentence you wish sounded different.

grade.notes: The first step ('pick a gym or decide to work out at home', 15 min) still forces a decision and is bigger than it needs to be; a 2-minute action like putting shoes by the door would suit an avoider better. plan.taskTitle: Establish a regular gym routine
plan.analysis: Create a manageable plan that starts with the smallest possible commitment, then gradually builds consistency through low-pressure weekly actions.

steps.title: Pick your gym or workout space
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes looking at one gym near your home or deciding to work out at home. No need to commit yet—just find one option that seems doable. This is just a quick search, not a decision.

steps.title: Get one piece of workout gear ready
steps.description: Gather just one item: gym shoes, shorts, or a t-shirt. Put it somewhere visible. You're not buying a whole wardrobe—just making it easy to start tomorrow.

steps.title: Go to the gym once (no workout plan needed)
steps.description: Visit the gym or your workout space for just 10-15 minutes. Walk around, sit on a machine, or do one easy thing. The goal is just to show up and see what it feels like. Don't overthink it.

steps.title: Schedule your next gym session
steps.description: Pick one specific day next week (maybe the same day you went) and write it down or set a phone reminder. That's it—just lock in one day.

steps.title: Do a super simple 15-minute workout
steps.description: Next gym visit, do something easy: 10 minutes on a cardio machine, a few stretches, or walk on the treadmill. Keep it so easy you feel like you could do more—that's the point. Don't aim for exhaustion.

steps.title: Plan two more gym days for the following week
steps.description: After your first real visit, pick two more days in the next week to go. Text a friend or add to your calendar. You're building a tiny habit, not a strict program.
steps.when: Right after your first easy workout

steps.title: Review and adjust (optional)
steps.description: After 2-3 weeks, spend 10 minutes thinking: Did it feel okay? What small thing could make it easier (better time of day, different gym, different activity)? Make one tiny adjustment if needed.

plan.taskTitle: Create a comprehensive LSAT study plan and begin systematic test prep
plan.analysis: Break LSAT prep into bite-sized daily actions covering diagnostic testing, targeted skill building, and full practice exams over 6 weeks, with early momentum building to prevent overwhelm.

steps.title: Take a diagnostic LSAT practice test
steps.description: Complete one full, untimed LSAT practice test to establish baseline score and identify weak areas. This single test gives you concrete data instead of guessing where to focus. Don't worry about your score—it's just a starting point.

steps.title: Review diagnostic results and create a simple study schedule
steps.description: Score your diagnostic test, identify which sections need work (Logic Games, Reading Comp, or Logical Reasoning), and map out 4-5 study days per week through November 14. Write it down visually so it feels manageable, not overwhelming.

steps.title: Master one Logic Games type
steps.description: Focus on just ONE type of logic game (sequencing, grouping, matching, etc.) for 30 minutes. Learn the setup, watch one tutorial, do 3-4 practice problems. You don't need to be perfect—just understand the pattern.

steps.title: Practice Logic Games daily for one week
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes each day (just one game type at a time) working through logic game problems. Small daily wins build momentum. Each session should feel quick and doable.

steps.title: Build Reading Comprehension accuracy with one passage per session
steps.description: Work through a single RC passage (15 minutes) and review your answers carefully (15 minutes). Don't try to do multiple passages—this focused approach prevents burnout and builds confidence.
steps.when: October 14-20 (3 sessions spread across the week)

steps.title: Strengthen Logical Reasoning with targeted drills
steps.description: Pick one LR question type (assumption, strengthen/weaken, etc.) and do 10 questions on it, reviewing each one. Rough accuracy is fine—consistency matters more than perfection. Rotate through different question types weekly.

steps.title: Take a second timed practice test and compare to diagnostic
steps.description: Complete another full LSAT under timed conditions. This is just data—not a judgment. You should see improvement in at least one section. Review 5-10 questions you got wrong to spot patterns.

steps.title: Intensive final push: alternate between drills and full practice tests
steps.description: For the final two weeks, alternate between 30-minute targeted drills (one skill per day) and full practice tests (every 3-4 days). Each activity is very specific, so your brain won't feel scattered. You've built the foundation—now you're just refining.

plan.taskTitle: Complete Chapter 2 Literature Review (25 pages) for Thesis
plan.analysis: Break the literature review into sequential phases: outline key themes, draft sections without perfecting, integrate sources, then refine—prioritizing completion over polish.

steps.title: Create a rough outline of literature review themes
steps.description: List 4-6 main themes or topics your literature review will cover. Don't worry about perfect organization—just brain-dump the major concepts and arguments you need to discuss. This takes 20 minutes and gives you a roadmap.

steps.title: Draft introduction section (rough version)
steps.description: Write 1-2 pages introducing your topic and explaining what the literature review will cover. Rough draft is fine—aim for clarity, not perfection. You're establishing context, not polishing prose.

steps.title: Draft first 2-3 literature sections
steps.description: Pick your first 2-3 themes and write rough paragraphs summarizing key papers and arguments under each. Don't aim for elegant writing; just get ideas on the page with citations. Speed over perfection.

steps.title: Draft remaining literature sections
steps.description: Complete the final 2-3 theme sections using the same rough-draft approach. Keep momentum by not re-reading or editing earlier sections yet. Done is better than perfect.

steps.title: Integrate citations and create bibliography
steps.description: Go through your draft sections and ensure all sources are properly cited. Run a citation tool to generate a clean bibliography. This is mechanical work and feels productive.

steps.title: Draft conclusion section
steps.description: Write a 1-2 page conclusion summarizing the literature landscape and how it connects to your thesis. Again, rough version—you're synthesizing, not perfecting.

steps.title: Read through full draft and make high-level revisions
steps.description: Do a single read-through focusing only on flow, gaps, and major clarity issues. Fix anything confusing, but don't obsess over word choice or sentence-level editing. This is structural review only.

steps.title: Final polish and proofreading
steps.description: Do a careful final pass for grammar, typos, and formatting consistency. This is your only dedicated editing pass. Remember: this chapter is a draft that will likely evolve—aim for 'good enough to submit' not 'publication-ready.'

plan.taskTitle: Schedule a dental cleaning appointment by calling the dentist

steps.title: Find the dentist's phone number
steps.description: Spend just 5 minutes looking up your dentist's contact information online or checking past appointment cards/emails. No pressure—this is just gathering info. If you don't have a dentist, do a quick search for one nearby.

steps.title: Write down what you'll say
steps.description: Jot down 3-4 bullet points: your name, that you need a cleaning, and your general availability (e.g., 'mornings work best'). This removes the anxiety of not knowing what to say. Keep it super casual.

steps.title: Make the call
steps.description: You've got this. Just dial the number and say what you wrote down. They handle this all day—it's easy for them. If you get voicemail, leave a message with your name and number. You're done.

plan.taskTitle: Update resume and LinkedIn profile for career fair

steps.title: Refresh LinkedIn profile headline and about section

steps.title: Update LinkedIn experience and skills sections

plan.taskTitle: Memorize the first 36 elements of the periodic table for chemistry quiz by Monday
plan.analysis: Break memorization into manageable chunks using varied techniques (mnemonics, flashcards, visual patterns, practice tests) over 4 days to keep things engaging and prevent boredom.

steps.title: Create a colorful periodic table visual with element groups highlighted
steps.description: Spend 15 focused minutes printing or drawing the first 36 elements on a large sheet, using different colors for alkali metals, halogens, noble gases, etc. This visual hook makes the table less intimidating and more interesting to study.

steps.title: Learn elements 1-18 using the classic 'Happy Henry Likes Beer But Could Not Obtain Four Nuts' mnemonic
steps.description: Memorize the first 18 elements using creative mnemonics and their positions. Spend exactly 20 minutes on this—no more. The time limit keeps you focused and prevents boredom from setting in.

steps.title: Learn elements 19-36 with custom mnemonics and grouping patterns
steps.description: Create or find mnemonics for K through Kr (potassium to krypton). Organize by chemical families to spot patterns. Spend 20 focused minutes and use rhythm/rhyme to make it stick.

steps.title: Make digital flashcards and test yourself on random elements
steps.description: Create 36 flashcards (symbol, name, atomic number). Use an app like Quizlet or physical index cards. Spend 15 minutes making them, then 10 minutes doing a quick quiz-yourself session. The interactive format beats passive review.

steps.title: Speed-run recall drills with timed challenges
steps.description: Set a timer for 10 minutes and write down as many elements as you can recall. Check your answers, identify weak spots, then do another 10-minute round focusing on those gaps. Make it gamified to stay engaged.

steps.title: Final confidence check and memory test the night before
steps.description: Do one last comprehensive quiz (write all 36 elements in 15 minutes, then check). If you nail it, you're done. If 2-3 are fuzzy, spend 5 extra minutes on just those. You're likely solid by now.

plan.taskTitle: Write a cover letter for the Google APM (Associate Product Manager) role
plan.analysis: Break the cover letter into distinct sections, gathering key information first, then drafting rough content without perfectionism, and finally polishing selectively to meet the Friday deadline.

steps.title: Gather materials and outline structure
steps.description: Collect the Google APM job description, your resume, and 2-3 key accomplishments you want to highlight. Rough out the cover letter structure: opening hook, 2-3 body paragraphs (why Google, why APM, key strengths), and closing. Remember: this outline doesn't need to be perfect, just a roadmap.

steps.title: Draft opening paragraph
steps.description: Write a rough first paragraph that introduces yourself and expresses genuine interest in the Google APM role. Don't worry about perfect phrasing—just get your core idea down. Aim for 3-4 sentences max.

steps.title: Draft body paragraphs on why Google and why APM
steps.description: Quickly write 2 rough paragraphs: one about why you're excited about Google specifically, and one about why product management appeals to you. These don't need to be polished—rough draft is fine at this stage.

steps.title: Draft paragraph highlighting key skills and accomplishments
steps.description: Write one paragraph that weaves in 2-3 specific accomplishments that demonstrate APM-relevant skills (data-driven thinking, stakeholder management, user empathy, etc.). Again, prioritize substance over perfect wording.

steps.title: Draft closing paragraph
steps.description: Write a brief closing paragraph that reiterates your enthusiasm and includes a soft call-to-action. Keep it concise (3-4 sentences). Done is better than perfect here.

steps.title: Read through and do one pass of refinement
steps.description: Read the entire draft aloud to catch awkward phrasing and clarity issues. Make targeted edits only—fix flow, remove jargon, strengthen weak sentences. Don't obsess over every word. Aim for 'good' not 'perfect.'

steps.title: Final proofread and format check
steps.description: Check for spelling, grammar, and formatting. Ensure it's 3/4 to 1 full page, has proper spacing, and uses a professional tone. This is your last stop—then submit it.

plan.taskTitle: Organize notes for all 5 classes before midterms

steps.title: Pick your most difficult class and organize its notes only
steps.description: Choose the one class where notes feel most scattered or confusing. Spend just 20 minutes sorting those notes chronologically or by topic. Don't worry about making it perfect—rough organization is totally fine. This builds momentum and removes the biggest source of stress.

steps.title: Organize second class notes with the same method
steps.description: Apply the same organizational approach to your second-most challenging class. This repetition makes it easier since you already know the process. You've got this—each class is just one small session.

steps.title: Tackle your third class notes
steps.description: Continue with class number three using your established system. You're halfway done with the hard part. Keep the standard rough-but-functional approach—don't second-guess yourself.

steps.title: Organize remaining two classes back-to-back

steps.title: Quick review and fill any obvious gaps
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes flipping through all five sets of organized notes to spot any missing dates, definitions, or key concepts. Add sticky notes for gaps—don't rewrite everything. This quick pass ensures nothing important was missed without adding stress.

steps.title: Create one master study checklist across all classes
steps.description: On one piece of paper or document, list 2-3 key topics per class that will likely be on the midterm. This gives you a simple roadmap for studying without feeling lost. Rough list only—this takes just 20 minutes.

plan.taskTitle: Develop comprehensive marketing plan for local coffee shop with team of 4

plan.taskTitle: Write a 3-page comparative essay on Plato vs. Aristotle's views on justice
plan.analysis: Start with easy research and note-taking, then organize a simple outline, then write each section incrementally to avoid feeling overwhelmed by the full task.

steps.title: Gather your thoughts for 10 minutes

steps.title: Quick skim of one source on each philosopher

steps.title: Write Aristotle section (1 page)

steps.title: Quick proofread and fix obvious issues
steps.description: Read through once, fix typos, check that paragraphs flow, ensure you hit 3 pages. You don't need perfection, just clarity. This usually takes 15-20 minutes.

grade.notes: The first step is a 30-minute review with no concrete starting action (e.g., open the assignment file and read problem 1), so it is too big and vague for a procrastinator. Step 2 requires finding outside practice problems, which adds decisions and busywork, and the plan never opens the assignment and data early; it also has a minor sequencing oddity with review after solving and a Monday final step that leaves little buffer.

plan.taskTitle: Complete 20 hypothesis testing problems in R
plan.analysis: Work through problems systematically in groups, starting with review of concepts, then solving practice problems, then tackling the full assignment with time for debugging and verification.

steps.title: Review hypothesis testing concepts and R syntax
steps.description: Review class notes and textbook on hypothesis testing (null/alternative hypotheses, p-values, significance levels). Refresh memory on key R functions like t.test(), prop.test(), and aov().

steps.title: Work through 5 practice problems with solutions
steps.description: Find and solve 5 example hypothesis testing problems using R, consulting solutions as needed. Focus on understanding the workflow: formulate hypotheses, run test, interpret p-value.

steps.title: Solve problems 1-7 from the assignment
steps.description: Complete the first 7 homework problems, writing clean R code with comments. Test each solution and verify outputs make sense statistically.

steps.title: Solve problems 8-14 from the assignment
steps.description: Continue with the next 7 problems. Take a 10-minute break halfway through to avoid fatigue and mental errors.

steps.title: Solve problems 15-20 and review all solutions
steps.description: Complete remaining 6 problems, then review all 20 solutions for consistency, proper formatting, and correct interpretation of statistical results.

steps.title: Debug errors and verify outputs
steps.description: Run through entire assignment, check for any R errors, ensure all code executes cleanly, and verify numerical answers are reasonable given the hypotheses and data.

steps.title: Final review and submission
steps.description: Do a final read-through for clarity and completeness, ensure all answers are labeled and explained, then submit before the 11:59pm deadline.
